title: Prices Keep Going Up
summary: Prices went up again last month. A new report says prices rose four-tenths of a percent. Food and energy cost more. Housing costs went up, too. Experts think prices will rise about 4 percent this year. That is faster than pay is rising, so family budgets feel tighter. Inflation means prices rising over time. When prices stay high, your money buys less. The Federal Reserve, America's central bank, wants inflation at 2 percent. Austan Goolsbee, who leads the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, called the report 'another distressing report, borderline disturbing.' He said the war in the Middle East has pushed up energy prices. The cost of tariffs on goods was supposed to fade, but it has not. Services like health care are also getting more costly. Food and housing are things families cannot skip. A farmer in Illinois even sent Goolsbee a diesel pump, saying prices are killing them. A new factor is the building of AI data centers, which pushes up the cost of computers and construction. Inflation has stayed above 2 percent for nearly six years.
why_it_matters: When prices rise faster than your family's pay, there is less money for food, clothes, and fun, so inflation touches your everyday life.

background_read: Inflation means prices rise over time, so the same money buys less than it used to.
America's central bank, the Federal Reserve, tries to keep inflation near 2 percent.
When food, energy, and housing cost more than pay grows, families feel squeezed because they cannot skip those costs.
Article_Structure: WHO: Austan Goolsbee, who leads the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, and experts who study prices.
WHAT: A new report says prices are still rising faster than pay, driven by food, energy, and housing.
WHERE: Across the United States, with a focus on the Midwest and a farmer in Illinois.
WHY: Because food, energy, housing, and services keep costing more, and demand from building AI data centers adds to the pressure.
